rewrites.summary:
Chad is dangerous for trans visitors — a high-risk verdict reached on thin data, not in spite of it. Consensual same-sex conduct between adults has been criminalised since 2017 as a misdemeanour carrying up to two years' imprisonment, so a trans visitor stands under formal criminal exposure — including one travelling with a partner. There is no legal gender recognition, no recourse, no protective or community infrastructure documented, and the state operates under junta-adjacent governance.

Enforcement of the criminalisation is not documented in either direction. That gap denotes an unknown, not safety: in a state that criminalises, denies recognition, offers no recourse and no documented protective or community infrastructure, the structural signals resolve toward danger, and the law remains usable against a visibly trans visitor at any time — arrest, prosecution and imprisonment of up to two years are live possibilities.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (up to 2 years) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

The drive sits in a regional pattern: parallel criminalisation attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda but succeeded in Chad and Nigeria within a broader conservative anti-LGBT advocacy wave. Before 2017 the law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts', with no documented use against LGBT persons; under the prior regime, abuses — extrajudicial killings, torture — are documented as general governance context.
rewrites.localsOnly: Pre-criminalisation baseline only: no known LGBT organisations, few reported acts of violence, and most people discreet due to social strictures — the documented resident-side climate, dating from before the 2017 law.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Very thin data: enforcement of the 2017 criminalisation in either direction is undocumented; no community or protective infrastructure is documented since criminalisation; the resident-side record rests on the pre-criminalisation baseline.
rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (misdemeanour, up to 2 years); military-adjacent governance; no legal gender recognition; no community infrastructure; very thin data.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (up to 2 years) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
blindSourceSummaries: A government annual human-rights report: the criminalisation section states the law criminalised consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment — official current-law baseline for visitor exposure; the report also covers societal abuses.

A government 2010 human-rights report (pre-criminalisation baseline): the law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts' with no evidence it was used against LGBT persons that year; no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, most persons discreet due to social strictures — documents the pre-2017 legal climate.
A government 2006 human-rights report: documents the then-regime's abuses — extrajudicial killings, torture, peacekeeping withdrawal — general context.

A news analysis: while further criminalisation attempts failed in some regional countries, they succeeded in this one and another — situates the country's criminalisation drive within the broader wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy, relevant context for how the law's trajectory developed.
rewrites.notes: Rule-8 thin-data rework: unknown not read as safe — structural signals (criminalisation, no LGR, no recourse, junta-adjacent governance) resolve toward danger; all prior sourced facts retained, no new facts. rewrites.summary:
Florida's 2023 facilities law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes remaining in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — once a government employee orders departure. It applies in every building owned or leased by the state or local government — offices, courthouses, legislative buildings, prisons/jails, parks and toll-road plazas — and purports to cover all schools, public or private, with only private businesses outside it. For every trans visitor whose document marker differs from presentation, this is universal, continuous exposure: every bathroom or changing-facility use inside a covered venue is a possible trigger, and the exposure holds regardless of how often the law is enforced.

The exposure is invoked, not hypothetical: in March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested for using a women's restroom in the State Capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state bathroom ban — and a Leon County judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 only on speedy-trial grounds after the state missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. That dismissal is a procedural outcome, not evidence of limited force: among at least 14 states with facility restrictions, only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself. Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning trans travellers and movers of the risks.

Legal exposure and street-level violence are independent visitor risks, and both are documented here: a July 2026 analysis over 2008–2025 data scores Florida 8.0 on an anti-trans law scale and labels the state 'Do Not Travel', while recording 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year — itself an undercount floor and below the average of the worst-law states.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Pride and civic visibility are being rolled back statewide — removal of Pride crosswalks, with Orlando residents defying the state — visibility conflicts affecting LGBT+ presence broadly rather than trans status specifically.

Nationally, the law-vs-violence analysis finds state law severity does not correlate with killing rates — a near-flat trendline across the 26 states with data — so this state's legal climate and street-level violence are separate risk dimensions. The April 2023 travel advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries and preceded events and conferences cancelling, with the national military considering redeployment for service members' families.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-side data: 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k residents per year recorded over 2008–2025 — an undercount floor and below the average of the worst-law states; the national analysis treats killing rates as independent of state law severity.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The travel advisory itself also cites non-trans laws (reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety repeals, curriculum censorship); those shape the general rights climate but do not move trans-specific visitor risk.

The ACLU of Florida describes the law as 'complex, confusing, and vague' and advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel for those it may reach; the statute's constitutionality remains untested — the dismissed case never reached it.
rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province's 2023 law makes it a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — to remain in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth after a government employee orders departure; a civil-liberties organisation calls it 'complex, confusing, and vague' and of limited actual coverage, and among at least 14 state/provinces with facility restrictions only two state/provinces criminalise the act itself.

In March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested using a women's restroom in the state/province capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state/province bathroom ban. A county judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 on speedy-trial grounds after the state/province missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. Two rights organisations have issued travel advisories warning of risks to trans travellers and movers.

Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: a July 2026 analysis puts this state/province's recorded killing rate for trans women at 3.7 per 100k per year, below the average of the worst-law state/provinces — itself an undercount floor.
rewrites.blindTangential: Pride and civic visibility are being rolled back state/province-wide — removal of Pride crosswalks, with residents defying the state/province — visibility conflicts affecting LGBT+ presence broadly rather than trans status specifically.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The travel advisory itself also cites non-trans laws (reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety repeals, curriculum censorship); those shape the general rights climate but do not move trans-specific visitor risk.
blindSourceSummaries: A civil-liberties organisation's know-your-rights guide on the 2023 restroom law: refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can be criminal trespass, but the law only applies in buildings owned or leased by the state/province or local government — state/province offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons/jails, local immigration detention, state/province parks and toll-road plazas — and purports to cover all schools, public or private. Private businesses are outside its scope; the organisation advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

A news outlet (2025): a 20-year-old trans college student was arrested at the state/province capitol after declaring an intention to break the law and entering a women's restroom — believed to be the first arrest under this state/province's transgender bathroom restrictions. The student faced a misdemeanor trespass charge punishable by up to 60 days in jail; at least 14 state/provinces have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

A news outlet (6 Jul 2025): on 20 Jun 2025 a county judge threw out the trespass case against the trans student on a legal technicality — as a defendant charged under the facilities law the student had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate — so the statute was never substantively tested. The student had been charged 19 Mar 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested the student washing hands in a women's restroom at the state/province capitol.

A local rights organisation's travel advisory (12 Apr 2023): the organisation took the 'unprecedented step' of warning about risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to this state/province, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people, reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks, and book bans/curriculum censorship. The advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries; the organisation reports events and conferences cancelling and notes the national military considering redeployment for service members' families.

A national law-vs-violence analysis (2008-2025 data): this state/province scores 8.0 on the anti-trans law scale with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year, labelled 'Do Not Travel'; the article's core finding is that state/province law severity does not correlate with killing rates (trendline nearly flat across the 26 state/provinces with data) — legal climate and street-level violence are independent visitor risks.
